title: Dynamics (part 3)
textbookText: In the exploration of particle motion, Sir Isaac Newton meticulously employed the scientific method to derive three foundational principles, famously recognized as Newton's Laws of Motion. These laws serve as the bedrock of classical mechanics, encapsulating the fundamental dynamics governing the behavior of objects in motion. The trio comprises the First Law of Motion, which delineates the inertia-based nature of objects; the Second Law of Physics, Grade 11 | 77

Motion, explicating the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration; and the Third Law of Motion, illuminating the reciprocal action and reaction between interacting bodies. These laws collectively form an interconnected framework, providing a comprehensive understanding of motion and serving as a cornerstone in the study of classical mechanics. 4.3.1 Newton’s First Law of Motion: Force is involved during changes in the state of your body. Unless there is a change in your state, no force is necessary, and you remain intact. In other words, force is required to change direction, come to rest, start motion, accelerate, or decelerate. If no force is applied during such changes, you remain in your original state. Sir Isaac Newton studied these phenomena in the motion of bodies and formulated a law known as Newton’s first law of motion.

Statement: Everybody remains in its own state unless an external force is acted upon. According to it, a body at rest will remain at rest, and a body in motion will continue moving with the same speed along a straight line unless acted upon by an external force. To change from rest to motion, or vice versa, to accelerate, decelerate, or change direction, an external agency, called force, is required. If the force isn’t acted, the body remains in its own state i.e, either at rest or in motion in a straight line.

Since the force appears as a role model to change the state of the body in the first law, the first law hence defines the force. The law is also known as the law of inertia because a body remains inert unless acted upon by a force. This property exhibited by the body is called inertia, hence the term 'law of inertia'.

Examples: i) When a bus at rest suddenly begins to move, the passengers lean backwards. According to the first law of motion, a force is exerted on the bus, causing it to move forward. However, the upper part of the passengers, not directly affected by the force, exhibit the property of inertia of rest. As a result, the passengers lean backwards. ii) When a moving bus suddenly stops, the passengers lean forward due to the inertia of motion, or as per the first law, a force acts on the bus causing it to come to a stop with the lower parts of the passengers attached to their seats. However, due to the absence of a force acting on the passengers directly, they tend to remain in motion and thus lean backward. iii) When a moving bus suddenly turns into a direction, the passengers lean in the opposite direction. This is due to the inertia of direction, or according to the first law, because no force is acting directly on the passengers. As the passengers continue their motion in the same straight line, they oppose the change in direction and consequently lean in the opposite direction. iv) Mangoes fall on shaking the mango tree. v) One takes a short run before jumping.

vi) If in an emergency, we need to jump off a moving bus while jumping off, an external force is applied to our legs (or feet), causing them to reach the targeted point, while no force is exerted on the upper part of the body. Consequently, the upper part of the body, continuing with the motion of the bus, tends to fall in the direction of the bus. Therefore, for a safe jump, one should jump in the direction of the moving bus. vii) A moving fan goes on slowing down and finally stops. It doesn’t violate the first law. viii) A rolling ball on the ground goes on slowing down and finally stops. It also doesn’t violate the first law.
4.3.2 Newton’s second law of motion Activity 4.2 Do and think about the following activities. i) Give a push or a pull to a man walking along the road and observe what happens to him.

Determine the change in his momentum. ii) Apply more force to the same activity and observe how the motion changes. Determine the change in momentum here as well. iii) Consider how the momentum changes if you suddenly fall on the road while walking. iv) Consider or experience whether momentum changes when someone slaps you. v) Consider the similar change when two vehicles suddenly collide.

larger force is applied, and the change occurs in the direction of the force applied. In other
